current_example.title: Example: Estimating a Variance or Standard Deviation

q-254665.name: Question 1
q-254665.problem:
A restaurant manager records the total time $20$ customers waited before they were seated. The results are presented in the table below. 

| Waiting time (minutes) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $4$ |
| $10\le x<15$ | $6$ |
| $15\le x<20$ | $7$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $3$ |

$$

$$

Assuming that the waiting times within each class interval are uniformly distributed, find an estimate of the mean waiting time $\overset{―}{x},$ rounded to **one decimal place**.

Rounded to one decimal place, $\overset{―}{x}≈$
{{field-1}} minutes.
q-254665.worked_solution:
Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, the mean can be estimated as follows:

$$
\overset{―}{x}≈\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot {m}_{i}
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class, and

- $n$ is the total number of observations.

To estimate the mean, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each class and the products of the midpoints and frequencies.

| Waiting time (minutes) | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${f}_{i}\cdot {m}_{i}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $4$ | $5$ | $20$ |
| $10\le x<15$ | $6$ | $12.5$ | $75$ |
| $15\le x<20$ | $7$ | $17.5$ | $122.5$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $3$ | $25$ | $75$ |

$$

$$

Finally, we sum the values in the last column and divide by $20$ (the total number of observations).

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & ≈\frac{20+75+122.5+75}{20} \\  & =\frac{292.5}{20} \\  & ≈14.6\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 14.6

q-46017.name: Question 2
q-46017.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266392/assets/e2ed2c96d7bcc3b00d8e00d754b9e8b2492e15df6bd568c06e9d25a9ce658a58.png)

An experiment consists of taking $14$ measurements of rainfall (in $\text{mm}$) during the rainy season in Africa. The results are presented above in the form of a histogram. Assuming that the rainfall measurements within each class interval are uniformly distributed, find an estimate of the mean rainfall, rounded to two decimal places.
q-46017.worked_solution:
Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, the mean can be estimated as follows:

$$
\overset{―}{x}≈\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot {m}_{i}
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class, and

- $n$ is the total number of observations.

To estimate the mean, we represent the given data as a table and add columns for the midpoints of each class and the products of the midpoints and frequencies.

| Rainfall ($\text{mm}$) | ${m}_{i}$ | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}\cdot {f}_{i}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $200\le r<250$ | $225$ | $3$ | $675$ |
| $250\le r<300$ | $275$ | $5$ | $1375$ |
| $300\le r<350$ | $325$ | $4$ | $1300$ |
| $350\le r<400$ | $375$ | $2$ | $750$ |

$$

$$

Finally, we sum the values in the last column and divide by $14$ (the total number of observations).

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{r} & ≈\frac{675+1375+1300+750}{14} \\  & =\frac{4100}{14} \\  & ≈292.86\,\text{mm}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

An experiment consists of taking 14 measurements of rainfall (in mm) during the rainy season in Africa. The results are presented above in the form of a histogram. Assuming that the rainfall measurements within each class interval are uniformly distributed, find an estimate of the mean rainfall, rounded to two decimal places.

a
320.25mm
b
230.56mm
c
292.86mm
d
196.53mm
e
305.65mm
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into K classes, the mean can be estimated as follows: x―≈1n∑i=1Kfi⋅mi where

  • fi is the frequency of the ith class,

  • mi is the midpoint of the ith class, and

  • n is the total number of observations.

To estimate the mean, we represent the given data as a table and add columns for the midpoints of each class and the products of the midpoints and frequencies.

Rainfall (mm) mi fi mi⋅fi
200≤r<250 225 3 675
250≤r<300 275 5 1375
300≤r<350 325 4 1300
350≤r<400 375 2 750

Finally, we sum the values in the last column and divide by 14 (the total number of observations).

r―≈675+1375+1300+75014=410014≈292.86mm

q-254738.name: Question 3
q-254738.problem:
Consider the frequency table below for a continuous variable $x.$ The total number of observations is $n=15,$ and the estimated sample mean is $\overset{―}{x}≈23.$

| Range | Frequency $({f}_{i})$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $2$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $4$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $4$ |
| $30\le x<40$ | $5$ |

$$

$$

Using the midpoint of each class interval to approximate all observations within that class, estimate the standard deviation ${\sigma }_{n},$ using $n$ as the denominator in the variance formula.

Rounded to one decimal place, ${\sigma }_{n}≈$
{{field-1}}
q-254738.worked_solution:
Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, we can estimate the variance by treating all observations within each class as though they were equal to the midpoint of that class. This gives

$$
{\sigma }_{n}^{2}≈\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot ({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class,

- $n$ is the total number of observations, and

- $\overset{―}{x}$ is the estimated mean, calculated using the class midpoints.

To find the variance, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each interval, the squared deviations of the midpoints from the mean, and the products of the squared deviations and frequencies.

| Range | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ | ${f}_{i}{({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $2$ | $5$ | $324$ | $648$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $4$ | $15$ | $64$ | $256$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $4$ | $25$ | $4$ | $16$ |
| $30\le x<40$ | $5$ | $35$ | $144$ | $720$ |

$$

$$

Then, we divide the sum of all the values in the last column by $15$ (the total number of observations):

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n}^{2} & ≈\frac{648+256+16+720}{15} \\  & =\frac{1640}{15} \\  & ≈109.3333\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the estimated standard deviation is the square root of the estimated variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n} & ≈\sqrt{109.3333}≈10.5\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 10.5

q-254806.name: Question 4
q-254806.problem:
A teacher wants to estimate the standard deviation of some students' grades on the final math exam. The following frequency table records the students' grades.

| Grades (${x}_{i}$) | Frequency $({f}_{i})$ |
| --- | --- |
| $50\le x<60$ | $2$ |
| $60\le x<70$ | $5$ |
| $70\le x<80$ | $10$ |
| $80\le x<90$ | $6$ |
| $90\le x<100$ | $5$ |

$$

$$

The estimated mean grade is $\overset{―}{x}≈77.5.$ Using the midpoint of each class interval to approximate all observations within that class, estimate the standard deviation ${\sigma }_{n},$ using $n$ as the denominator in the variance formula.

Rounded to one decimal place, ${\sigma }_{n}≈$
{{field-1}}.
q-254806.worked_solution:
Given a frequency table containing data split into $K$ classes, we can estimate the variance by treating all observations within each class as though they were equal to the midpoint of that class. This gives

$$
{\sigma }_{n}^{2}≈\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot ({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class,

- $n$ is the total number of observations, and

- $\overset{―}{x}$ is the estimated mean, calculated using the class midpoints.

To find the variance, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each interval, the squared deviations of the midpoints from the mean, and the products of the squared deviations and frequencies.

| ${x}_{i}$ | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ | ${f}_{i}{({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $50\le x<60$ | $2$ | $55$ | $506.25$ | $1012.5$ |
| $60\le x<70$ | $5$ | $65$ | $156.25$ | $781.25$ |
| $70\le x<80$ | $10$ | $75$ | $6.25$ | $62.5$ |
| $80\le x<90$ | $6$ | $85$ | $56.25$ | $337.5$ |
| $90\le x<100$ | $5$ | $95$ | $306.25$ | $1531.25$ |

$$

$$

Then, we divide the sum of all the values in the last column by the total number of observations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n}^{2} & ≈\frac{1012.5+781.25+62.5+337.5+1531.25}{2+5+10+6+5} \\  & =\frac{3725}{28} \\  & ≈133.0357\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the estimated standard deviation is the square root of the estimated variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n} & ≈\sqrt{133.0357}≈11.5\end{aligned}
$$
